To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the CeHSF‐2 protein is an HSF‐1‐like protein that binds to the heat shock element in the promoter of hsp70 gene in C. elegans.

the HSF1 protein of C. elegans is a heat‐sensitive transcription factor that binds DNA as a homodimer and is capable of binding to the HSEs in both the promoter and coding regions of the Hsp‐16.2 gene.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular basis of the regulation of gene expression during development.
understanding the molecular mechanisms of DNA binding and regulation of transcription factor function, and how they are altered in human disease.
the identification of the transcription factors involved in the heat shock response and their role in regulating the expression of heat shock proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HSFs are not only transcription factors but also play an important role in protein folding and degradation of proteins.
CeHSF‐2 physically interacts with CeHsp70‐3 by a cross‐linking assay, and this physical interaction is required for its DNA binding activity.
CeHSF‐2 and CeHSF‐3 are the most similar to Drosophila HSFs, while the CeHSF‐4 and CeHSF-6 have the highest similarity to HSFs of other species, including mammals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we identified a new HSF‐like protein in C. elegans, which we called CeHSF‐2.
we have found that the heat shock response in C. elegans is regulated by a complex network of transcription factors that include HSF‐1 and HSF‐3.

HSFs from different organisms recognize different DNA motifs, and that the HSFs from model organisms have evolved to be more divergent than those from other organisms, which may reflect their different evolutionary history.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the heat shock response is not just a simple on/off switch, and that it has a much more complex and dynamic role than previously thought.
the HSFs from model organisms are not interchangeable in terms of DNA binding specificity, despite sharing similar overall structures and binding modes.
HSFs from different organisms recognize the same core DNA sequence but have different DNA binding specificities, suggesting that the HSF‐DNA interaction is not as conserved as previously thought.
